items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: when I was with Troy First, joined Troy Floyd's band

ctx.x: Well, some people are great readers but can't play, you know. That's true.

Yeah. A lot of, well, for instance, for a long time, when I was with Troy First, joined Troy Floyd's band, I didn't have too much time for solo work. Yeah. Most of mine was reading because the fellas in the band were limited. And of course, naturally, I had to play three, four, five different parts. Yeah. But as the band got older and we got to playing together, well then I could occasionally get out and solo.
Mm-hmm. Well, you must have been an awful good soloist, changing from the rapids. There's so many things.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1969-12-30
items.q: So I got the job from just him and him. He blew my horn. And he was a man. He became the first chair man, also the feature man, because out of 10 musicians...

ctx.x: And another thing he asked me about it was this Wabash Blues was supposed to be out by Troy Floyd, I guess.

Now, that's a little controversial there. Yeah. As far as I know, Troy did not make this Wabash Blues, but I have a copy of it at my home in San Antonio. I can't recall who the musicians on there just by playing it, but it seems to me that I can remember that I was part of that Wabash Blues, I'm not for sure, and also Charlie Dixon. When we recorded all these numbers, even with Hattie Brothers and the whole group, I think we recorded about three or four days. And the same musicians that were on these recordings…
Well, tell me a little bit more about Troy Floyd's band. I don't know too much about it, it's what you've told me.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: Troy just told me, well, come on, you'll go on the job with me... I got the job with Troy.

ctx.x: Oh, yes. I knew him. Very much in Chicago.

That's right. Well, Lee was playing in the same neighborhood. And that's when Troy Floyd came to town. And I was a fellow who always liked to follow musicians. And I happened to go to a party I was having there for Troy. Troy was a great man then. And I got to talking to some of the guys in his band and also Trent's band. So Chester Clark, which is another great trumpet player, said, why don't you try to get that job with Troy's band? He says, Claude Kennedy's leaving. Oh, I says, I don't know if I could play…
After having that self-edged training for a year and a half, that comes to see for you.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-12-30
items.q: It was a job that Troy Floyd was on... So I took the job... well not with my band, with Troy.

ctx.x: We were talking about the Dallas State Fair, how your band got started there. What went on at the Dallas State Fair? See, I never was at a...

Well, that's every October. That's a regular, one of the regular celebrations that they have. The world's fast stage fair. And this year, I don't remember what year it was that I was playing with. But it was in October of 1929. And the band that organized in New Orleans out there, Bernard Goldberg, had given me that money. We drove all the way from New Orleans, all the way from New Orleans into Dallas. And that was... Well, maybe I'll say that the Lord's blessed me more ways when one, it was... This was the only…
So you added men once the State Fair was over?
